guideTitle: 6 Best Large-Button Calculators for Low Vision in 2026
metaTitle: 6 Best Large-Button Calculators for Low Vision
metaDescription: Six large-button calculators for visually impaired users, comparing talking models, dual-line screens, 5-inch displays, and key size and contrast.
introParagraphs: A calculator for low vision has two jobs: show numbers big enough to read, or say them out loud when reading fails. Large keys then keep your fingers on target while you work. The six picks below split into talking models and big-screen silent models, so you can choose the support that matches how much sight you rely on.

We evaluated each pick from the product listings and buyer feedback, focusing on voice output, dual-line displays, screen size and angle, key size, and power. Four of the six speak, one offers a 5-inch silent screen, and one is a simple eight digit unit for those who need only big keys. We treat these as everyday household tools, not medical devices, and we make no medical claims.
Decide first whether you need to hear your entries, then use the tables to narrow to the right model.

products.badge: Designed With Low Vision in Mind
products.name: The Low Vision Store Two-Line Talking Calculator
products.description:
This is the only listing here that says it was built for people with low vision, including seniors and those who cannot see the screen at all. Its two-line LCD is large and shows your inputs and your results at the same time. The voice announcement speaks numbers, function keys, and results, so you hear the whole operation and not only the answer.

Hearing the function key as well as the digit is the detail that matters. If you press the plus key by mistake, the speech tells you before you reach equals. The listing gives fewer specifics about key size and power than the others, so buyers should read the full page before ordering.

It is a purpose-built aid, so there is little decoration to learn around. Plan on keeping the volume down in shared rooms, since every key announces itself. Compared with the iPepul, this unit announces functions explicitly, and compared with the Cirbic, it leans harder on an accessibility identity than on keypad extras.
products.bestFor: People who cannot rely on the screen and want every key press announced out loud.

Large two-line LCD shows inputs and results together
Built around low vision use rather than adapted to it
Simple operation with little to learn around
cons: Listing gives few details on key size and power
Every key press is audible in a shared room

products.name: Cirbic Loud and Clear Talking Calculator
products.description:
The Cirbic talking desk calculator is marketed for visually impaired users and gives you speech with a wide volume range. You can mute it for quiet work or push it loud for a noisy room. It announces numbers and results, and its dual-line LCD keeps the current entry and last answer in view.

What sets it apart is the high contrast key set. Keys that stand out against the body are easier to locate by sight for those with partial vision, and oversized tops reduce mispresses. It does not list a stated screen tilt or specific dimensions, so shoppers who care about angle will need to check the listing photos.

For day to day use, the mute to loud range is useful in a library, a waiting room, or a bustling kitchen. Compared with the MAUJOY it puts more emphasis on volume range, while compared with the pendancy it trades screen scale for voice. If you want a talking calculator that is also friendly to partial sight, this is a strong fit.
products.bestFor: People with partial sight who want speech and high contrast keys together.
pros: Volume adjusts from mute to loud for any setting
High contrast keys stand out against the body
Dual-line LCD keeps entry and last result visible
Oversized keys reduce mispresses on every entry
cons: Listing gives no stated screen tilt or dimensions
Voice may disturb others in a quiet shared room

products.name: iPepul 2-Line Talking Desktop Calculator
products.description:
iPepul combines a voice broadcast function with a two-line, twelve digit LCD set at a fixed 45 degree angle. After each input, the calculator reads out the numbers and results. The steep tilt is meant to reduce neck strain, which suits those who bend to see the screen.

The fixed 45 degree angle is steeper than the 30 degree tilt of the pendancy, so a person seated low may find the view more direct. The keys are large and the layout is limited to four functions, which cuts down on confusion. The downside is that a fixed angle cannot be adjusted if your seat and desk do not match it.

The voice reads after each input, so you hear a digit before you press the next. That steady feedback makes a typo easy to catch. Compared with the Low Vision Store model, the iPepul gives you an explicit angled screen, but the Low Vision Store speaks function keys too.
products.bestFor: People who sit low or bend to see the screen and also want digits read aloud.

Fixed 45 degree display faces a seated reader
Two-line 12 digit LCD shows previous calculation
Four function layout keeps the key face plain
cons: Fixed tilt cannot adjust to different desk heights
Four functions only, with no percent or memory

products.name: MAUJOY Talking Desk Calculator
products.description:
MAUJOY builds a high quality voice broadcasting system into a desk calculator aimed at visually impaired users. It offers real-time audio feedback, a twelve digit dual-line display, and big buttons. Beyond addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division, it handles percentages and square roots.

Percent and square root are the reason to pick it over the more basic talking models. Someone working out a discount or a tax rate can do it without a second device. The tradeoff is a slightly fuller key face to learn, and the listing leaves out specifics such as screen angle and battery type.

In daily use, the audio keeps pace with your input, so you can check each digit before you proceed. Keep the volume modest when others are nearby. Against the iPepul, the MAUJOY offers percent and square root where the iPepul stays at four functions, and against the Cirbic it competes on functions rather than volume range.
products.bestFor: Talking calculator users who also need percent and square root for discounts or rates.

Big buttons help limit wrong-key presses
cons: Listing omits screen angle and battery details

products.name: pendancy 5-Inch Big Number Calculator
products.description:
If you have some sight and prefer silence, the pendancy gives you a 5-inch LCD with twelve large digits. The display is tilted at 30 degrees so it faces you at the desk. Keys are giant and color coded, which helps locate the right group by hue.

Color grouping is a quiet aid for low vision. Orange, blue, and gray key sets let you find the operator area without reading labels. The pendancy does not speak, so a person who cannot read even a 5-inch screen will want a talking model instead.

The body is lightweight ABS plastic, which is easy to move but can slide when you press hard. Put it on a mat or a nonslip surface if you notice that. Compared with the talking picks here, it offers the largest silent display, and compared with the CATIGA 8-digit model it brings far more screen at the cost of desk space.
products.bestFor: People with usable sight who want a huge silent screen and color cues for the keys.
pros: 5 inch LCD gives the biggest silent display here
Color coded key groups can be found by hue alone
30 degree tilt faces you when seated at a desk
Giant response keys give wide press targets
cons: No voice output if the screen is still unreadable

products.name: CATIGA 8 Digit Solar Big Button Calculator
products.description:
CATIGA's eight digit model is the stripped down option, with a large screen, a tilted display, and large responsive buttons. Spacious key sizes mean your fingers are less likely to hit the wrong number. The body is sturdy plastic built for everyday use.

Eight digits is fewer than the twelve found on the other picks, and for most household sums that is still plenty. What you gain in return is larger numerals per screen width and a lighter learning load. Power is solar, so you should place it where light reaches the panel.

It does not speak and it does not magnify beyond a large standard screen, so it is not for severe vision loss. It does suit someone who needs big keys and a calm layout more than a talking assistant. Compared with the pendancy, it is smaller and quieter to use, and compared with the talking models it offers no audio but asks for much less attention.
products.bestFor: People who need roomy keys and an easy to read display but no speech.

Tilted, angled screen reduces how far you lean in

cons: Eight digits is fewer than the twelve on other picks

buyingCriteria.explanation: The most important question is whether you can read the screen at all. If digits blur even at a large size, a talking calculator is the right tool. The Low Vision Store, Cirbic, iPepul, and MAUJOY all speak, while the pendancy and CATIGA 8 Digit rely on sight. If you can read a 5-inch display, a silent model avoids the noise.

Not every talking calculator speaks the same things. The Low Vision Store model announces numbers, functions, and results, while the iPepul reads numbers and results after each input. Hearing the function key lets you catch a wrong operator before equals. Check what the listing says, since a result-only voice leaves a gap.

A voice you cannot turn down becomes a nuisance, and a voice you cannot turn up fails in a noisy room. The Cirbic runs from mute to loud, which is the widest stated range here. Think about a library, a kitchen, and a shared office. If you work around others, volume control matters more than any other voice feature.

A two-line display shows your current entry above the previous result, which helps catch errors. The iPepul sits at a fixed 45 degree angle, the pendancy at 30 degrees, and the CATIGA 8 Digit uses a tilted screen. A steeper tilt helps a low seated reader, but a fixed angle cannot be changed. Match the angle to the chair and desk you will actually use.

For partial sight, key contrast helps as much as size. The Cirbic lists high contrast oversized keys, the pendancy uses orange, blue, and gray groups, and the CATIGA 8 Digit lists large responsive buttons. Aim for keys you can find by color or feel, not just by reading a label. Avoid low contrast keys where labels fade into the body.

More digits on a fixed screen width usually means smaller numerals. The CATIGA 8 Digit trades four digits for bigger ones, while the others offer twelve. Household sums rarely need more than eight. If your use is shopping and bills, fewer, larger digits are a smart tradeoff.

howWeEvaluated.title: Voice and spoken feedback
howWeEvaluated.description: We read what each listing says the voice announces: digits, function keys, or only results. The Low Vision Store scored highest for naming functions as well. The Cirbic, iPepul, and MAUJOY announce numbers and results, and volume control was counted separately. Silent models were judged in a different category rather than penalized.

howWeEvaluated.title: Display readability
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed screen size, line count, and angle. The pendancy leads silent models at 5 inches and 30 degrees, and the iPepul has a fixed 45 degree angle with two lines. The Cirbic, MAUJOY, and Low Vision Store all list dual or two-line displays. We did not measure digit height, so scores reflect specs and buyer feedback.

howWeEvaluated.title: Key size and contrast
howWeEvaluated.description: Key size, contrast, and color cues were scored together as a finding aid for partial sight. The Cirbic earned marks for high contrast, the pendancy for color grouping, and the CATIGA 8 Digit for spacious responsive buttons. Listings that did not mention contrast were scored on size alone. We favored layouts that avoid tiny labels.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ease of use and learning
howWeEvaluated.description: A calculator that needs a long manual defeats the purpose. The iPepul with four functions and the CATIGA 8 Digit score best for simplicity. The MAUJOY adds percent and square root, which adds a little learning. Everything was weighed against how little someone must memorize.

howWeEvaluated.title: Lineup positioning
howWeEvaluated.description: The Low Vision Store leads on accessibility, with spoken functions and a low vision focus, and the Cirbic leads on volume range. The iPepul leads on screen angle with a fixed 45 degrees, the MAUJOY on functions, and the pendancy on silent screen size at 5 inches. The CATIGA 8 Digit leads on simplicity. Choose by which gap in your vision matters most.

faq.q: Do I need a talking calculator if I have low vision?
faq.a: Not always. If a 5-inch screen like the pendancy's is readable, a silent model works and avoids noise. If digits blur or you have to guess, speech is the better aid. Many talking models can be muted, so they cover both cases.

faq.q: What is the difference between voice that reads results and voice that reads functions?
faq.a: A result-only voice speaks the answer, while a fuller voice also names the keys you press. The Low Vision Store model announces numbers, functions, and results, which helps you catch a wrong operator. Models like the iPepul read numbers and results after each input. Pick the fuller option if you often press the wrong operator.

faq.q: Why does a two-line display help?
faq.a: The top line shows your running calculation while the bottom shows the current entry or result, so you can check work without redoing it. The Cirbic, iPepul, MAUJOY, and Low Vision Store models all list dual or two-line screens. It is especially useful when voice and eyes both contribute. Single line screens force you to remember earlier steps.

faq.q: Are color coded keys really useful for low vision?
faq.a: They can be, because color groups help you find an area without reading labels. The pendancy uses orange, blue, and gray groups. Contrast matters too, so the Cirbic's high contrast keys offer a similar benefit in another form. Combine color with a firm sense of key position.

faq.q: Does the screen angle matter if I mostly listen?
faq.a: Less, but it still helps on days when your sight is better. A 45 degree iPepul display or a 30 degree pendancy display faces you, which saves your neck. Talking models are often used with partial sight, so the screen is not irrelevant. If you only listen, angle is a minor factor.

faq.q: Will a solar calculator work in a dim room?
faq.a: Solar alone may struggle in poor light, which is why many models add a battery. The CATIGA 8 Digit relies on solar power, so place it by a window or under a lamp. Check each listing for power details, and keep a spare cell on hand.

faq.q: Should I buy one of these for a family member?
faq.a: Ask what frustrates them now: reading digits, hitting keys, or hearing the answer. Then match the pick, using the tables above. A talking unit is a safe choice if they are unsure, since the volume can be turned down. Let them try it and keep the return window in mind.
